Set up & run

Parallel and scheduled runs

Sigma can run several things at once, and a timer can start it while another run is still going. This page explains how overlapping runs are kept from colliding, which settings widen the work, and how to start Sigma from a scheduler or from Codex.

On this page

  • Two kinds of parallel work
  • The settings
  • Slices of one goal
  • Several goals at once

  • The Codex supervisor

Most people only need

  • Leave both parallel switches off to start. Each ships off, and every goal then runs as one unit.
  • If you turn on goal-level parallelism, size parallel.goals.max_concurrent to your machine’s memory, not to how many issues are open.
  • For a scheduler, make the first step a check for a running session; if one is live, stop.
  • Pass the invoking shell’s own process id to every call a routine makes.

When triggers overlap

Sigma does not schedule itself. Whatever fires an agent on a timer (a desktop routine, a cron job, a hosted scheduler) does that. What Sigma provides is a safe answer to “is a session already running?”, so a routine can be set once and left alone without launching a second session on top of the first.

The answer comes from the session registry. When a run starts it records the process id of its long-lived caller, not of any one short-lived Sigma command, which exits within moments. A routine firing asks the registry first.

One firing, two outcomes. Several sessions register independently, and one ending never erases another’s entry.

  • ACTIVE means at least one registered process is alive and its lease is fresh.
  • FREE means every entry is absent, has a dead process, or has an expired lease.
  • A pick skips goals another live session has claimed, and each session keeps its own budgets and its own verify evidence, so one session starting never voids another’s passing verify.
  • In Codex Desktop, separate tasks can share a parent process id, so their entries are also keyed by the task’s thread id. If one task dies while the shared process lives, its entry expires after the lease time (12 hours by default); a clean exit clears it sooner. An unreadable marker also fails closed until its lease expires.

Two kinds of parallel work

There are two separate switches, and they do different things. Neither depends on the other.

Slices of one goalSeveral goals
What runs at onceIndependent slices of a single goal’s plan.Separate backlog goals, each from research to pull request.
Switchparallel.enabledparallel.goals.enabled
Widthparallel.max_concurrentparallel.goals.max_concurrent
IsolationEach slice that declares files gets its own worktree.Each goal gets its own worktree, branch and pull request. Needs work.enabled.
ConflictsSlices whose file lists can overlap never run together.No conflict check; overlap shows up later as an ordinary pull-request rebase.

The settings

KeyDefaultWhat it does
parallel.enabledoff (opt-in)Run one goal’s independent slices concurrently, in waves.
parallel.max_concurrent3The widest wave of slices. It never affects how many goals run.
parallel.goals.enabledoff (opt-in)Let a batch pick return several goals at once. With it off, or with only one goal available, a batch is the same as a single pick.
parallel.goals.max_concurrent3The most goals returned in one batch. A whole number of at least 1; a value that is not a number reads as 3.
handoff.after_goals20The orchestrating session stops claiming after this many goals, counting goals already done and goals still running.
budget.max_iterations20Goals per session; the free slots in a batch are also bounded by what is left of this.
resource.max_goalsno extra capHard cap on concurrent goals from the resource guard.

Only the JSON boolean true turns a switch on; a stray string or the number 1 does not. The rest of the settings are on All settings.

Slices of one goal

A goal is planned as slices, and by default they run one after another. With parallel.enabled on, you describe the slices in a file beside the plan, and Sigma groups the ones that cannot collide into waves.

[
  {"id": "s0", "title": "extract the config reader", "files": ["config/**"]},
  {"id": "s1", "title": "rewrite the loader", "needs": ["s0"], "files": ["engine/loader.py"]},
  {"id": "s2", "title": "new CLI flag", "needs": ["s0"], "files": ["cli/**"]}
]

This goes in .sdlc/plans/<goal-stem>.slices.json. needs, files, size and status are optional.

  • Waves, not a thread pool. Each wave packs slices that are runnable and do not conflict, up to parallel.max_concurrent. The order is deterministic, so you can read the plan before anything runs.
  • The conflict rule is cautious. Two slices conflict when their file patterns could overlap. A slice that declares no files conflicts with everything and runs alone. Every slice that declares files runs in its own worktree.
  • Slices run as subagents. A slice marked "size": "large", too big for one subagent’s context, is not run for you. The plan prints the exact command for you to start in a session of its own, and the loop never starts it. It also never starts an unattended second worker on the same .sdlc folder.

Several goals at once

With parallel.goals.enabled on, a batch pick returns up to parallel.goals.max_concurrent goals, and each is dispatched to its own subagent. The target is one person on one machine working through a stack of their own assigned issues. It is not a team coordination mechanism; the team ledger does that.

  • When a goal finishes, its slot is refilled with a new pick that names the goals still running. That naming is required: without it two subagents could take the same goal.
  • With work.enabled off, a batch is clamped to one goal, because concurrent goals are isolated only by their own worktrees.
  • A goal that a batch claimed but never dispatched keeps its in-progress mark. loop.py release removes the mark and leaves an audit comment without touching the goal label or spending any of the iteration budget.
  • On a host without subagents, goals run one at a time, inline.

The loop that drives these is described on Running many goals.

Scheduled and routine runs

A routine is any recurring trigger your host provides. The prompt it fires should do four things, in order:

  1. Check for a live session

    Run the session check. If it prints ACTIVE, stop. Nothing else happens in this firing.

  2. Start a session

    If it prints FREE, start one, passing the invoking shell’s own parent process id. Read that id fresh on every call.

  3. Drain by picking, never by remembering

    Ask for the next goal each time. Do not phrase the prompt as “continue where you left off”: a fresh firing has no transcript of the one before, and memory must never stand in for a real backlog pick.

  4. End the session

    When it stops, end the session with the same process id, so the next firing sees FREE.

The commands a routine prompt contains, with <installed-sigma> standing for the folder the plugin is installed in:

python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/loop.py session-active .sdlc
g=$(python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/loop.py start .sdlc --session-pid "$PPID")
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/loop.py session-end .sdlc --session-pid "$PPID" --session-generation "$g"

The process id appears on every call on purpose. Sigma cannot compute, from inside a short-lived command, a value that is both stable across your routine’s separate commands and unique to this firing. By default the fallback is the immediate parent, which is correct only for one continuous caller; a routine that runs each command separately gets a fresh parent every time. “Zero-touch” describes the scheduling and the fact that the prompt needs no per-firing edits, not the absence of the flag.

What to set first

For an unattended drain, turn on backlog_check.enabled. It is what makes a dependency marker written only as a comment, by a person, actually honoured instead of silently ignored. Keep the budgets in place; each belongs to the session that started it, so overlapping sessions can together spend several times one ceiling. The longer unattended walk-through is Running unattended.

The Codex supervisor

A Codex supervisor is a separate, opt-in path. It changes Codex behaviour only: it does not install, update or restart Claude Code, and the Claude supervisor and its review and model defaults are untouched. Sigma refuses to start it rather than guess.

What it refuses on

  • Sigma is not enabled in the current Codex home, or its version or installed source cannot be verified. It never borrows a checkout or a Claude plugin path.
  • A git-based marketplace install whose checkout or cached plugin is not clean, or is not at the same commit. On Windows this preflight currently refuses; it has been exercised on macOS only.
  • The Codex-enabled Sigma and the running Sigma differ in version. The supervisor refuses (“update the older host”); the doctor only warns.
  • The Codex command is ambiguous or invalid: an invalid SIGMA_CODEX_BIN refuses and never falls through, and two copies with different real paths refuse as ambiguous until you choose one.
  • A worker that exits with no final message, or with a message the supervisor cannot trust. A zero exit alone is not accepted as a finished goal.
  • A non-numeric SIGMA_SUPERVISE_MAX_RUNS or SIGMA_SUPERVISE_SLEEP_SCALE.
  • A second Codex supervisor for the same .sdlc folder: a kernel lock keeps it to one. A newly launched Claude worker does not take that lock, so do not run both supervisors for one checkout.

Starting it

  1. Check what is running

    Look at your config, current workers and the Codex plugin list. If a supervisor is already running for this checkout, stop it through its stop file and let it exit. Keep a backup of your config.

  2. Install in Codex only

    Add Sigma to Codex through its marketplace and confirm there is one enabled Sigma entry in the plugin list.

  3. Refresh the standing rules

    Refresh the Codex standing rules with the setup script’s Codex option (the Codex autonomy guide names it), then read the managed block it writes. This does not edit Claude’s files.

  4. Run one bounded smoke

    Run the supervisor once in a disposable repository or a small backlog with the run limit set to 1, then read the supervisor log, the exit code, the issue and pull-request trail and the final report before raising the limit.

  5. Opt in to a longer run

    On a laptop that sleeps, keep it awake. Stop it politely by creating .sdlc/state/supervisor.stop, and remove that file before a later restart.

The Codex supervisor uses an approval mode rather than an unrestricted sandbox bypass. Where a fresh Codex reviewer and automatic model tier are wanted for Codex only, the per-host override keys on All settings do that without changing the values Claude uses.

The resource guard

Parallel work is limited by the machine, not only by the settings above. Sigma reads memory, load and cores and derives its own limits; nothing is a constant copied from a laptop, and nothing here pauses a running process.

  • Admission, not interruption. A goal pick, a model session and a verify each take a lease first. With no room, the answer is a hold with a reason and a retry time. The picker leaves goals unclaimed; a verify exits with code 5 and the prefix RESOURCE-HOLD without running or writing evidence. The goal is not failed.
  • It narrows a batch. The number of goals a batch returns is the smallest of your configured width, what the machine has room for, and what is left under the hand-off and iteration ceilings.
  • A hold is a wait. A run that hits one waits and verifies again; it never edits code for it and never counts it as a review cycle. After six holds in a row the goal is parked. That bound is provisional, not derived from a measured hold.
  • Shed. Under sustained critical pressure the verify processes Sigma started are stopped. A model session is never signalled.
  • Modes. resource.mode is enforce, observe (log the would-be hold, admit) or off; the SIGMA_RESOURCE_MODE environment variable overrides it everywhere.

The guard cannot cover tests you run by hand outside the verify command, memory used by other programs, a host’s own subagent fan-out, or Windows (where it refuses rather than guess). The keys are on All settings and the unattended behaviour on Running unattended.

What is not measured

  • The resource-guard fractions are policy ratios, not fitted to a real exhaustion. Two recorded runs, on macOS and on Linux in a 2 GiB container, fixed none of them.
  • Memory is the dominant cost of running goals in parallel: each active goal is a full agent session, far heavier than an idle chat. parallel.goals.max_concurrent is effectively a memory knob. Token use is a separate axis; measure input, cached input, output and completed goals before claiming savings.
  • A Codex quota exhaustion and a full Codex goal-to-merge run have not been measured. The supervisor’s quota classifier has been exercised on synthetic text only.
  • The ledger’s per-process entry files and the local action logs grow for the life of a repository and nothing prunes them; this is correctness-neutral but is a read cost that rises.
